entities.name: Po Binasuor
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Po Binasuor, known in Vietnamese chronicles as Chế Bồng Nga and by other names such as Ngo-ta Ngo-che and Cei Bunga, presided over the last golden age of the Champa kingdom from 1360 to 1390 CE. His reign marked a formidable resurgence of Cham power, challenging the Đại Việt (later Vietnam) to an unprecedented degree and temporarily reversing decades of territorial losses. Unlike his predecessor Po Binnasuar, who ruled Panduranga (southern Champa) from 1316 to 1361, Po Binasuor consolidated control over the entire Cham realm and projected its military might far beyond its traditional borders, establishing himself as one of Southeast Asia's most dynamic and feared monarchs of the late medieval period. His aggressive expansionism fundamentally reshaped the geopolitical landscape of Indochina, initiating a protracted period of conflict that would ultimately contribute to Champa's decline, even as it showcased its martial prowess.

Under Po Binasuor's leadership, Champa launched a series of devastating campaigns against Đại Việt, culminating in the sacking of its capital, Thăng Long (modern-day Hanoi), on at least three occasions in 1371, 1377, and 1383 CE. The 1377 campaign was particularly significant, resulting in the death of Trần Duệ Tông, the Đại Việt emperor, at the Battle of Đồ Bàn (also known as Vijaya). Po Binasuor's military strategy often involved swift naval movements and coordinated land assaults, utilizing Champa's strong seafaring traditions. He also successfully repelled a major Đại Việt counter-invasion in 1378 and maintained Champa's independence against the burgeoning Ming dynasty, which demanded tribute. His reign was characterized by a robust military and a centralized administration that effectively mobilized resources for his expansionist agenda.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Po Binasuor's reign marked Champa's last major resurgence, challenging Đại Việt's dominance and leading to the death of an emperor, profoundly impacting regional power dynamics for decades. His campaigns delayed Vietnamese expansion and solidified Champa's martial reputation, albeit at a high long-term cost.
